OPENCODE TASKS

1. Inspect the repository and document the existing architecture
What to do:
Inspect the repository before changing application code. Identify the frontend, backend, database or storage layer, import pipelines, existing activity schemas, test framework, configuration files, source data directories, FIT/CSV handling, and deployment commands. Do not delete or overwrite existing data. Record the findings and implementation constraints.

Where:
Repository root: benpioske-del/garmin-export. Create or update docs/IMPLEMENTATION_INVENTORY.md.

How to verify success:

docs/IMPLEMENTATION_INVENTORY.md exists.
It identifies the relevant application entry points, data models, import code, test commands, and build commands.
It lists all discovered CSV, FIT, JSON, database, and configuration files relevant to activity data.
It explicitly records whether GPS coordinates, time zones, raw FIT files, and existing strength or health data were found.
The document does not claim that a file or feature exists unless inspection confirms it.
Priority: HIGH

2. Implement canonical activity records with provenance and data-quality status
What to do:
Create or extend the application's canonical activity model so each activity preserves:

Stable canonical identifier
Source file or source integration identifier
Original source timestamp
UTC timestamp
Athlete-local timestamp
Athlete-local calendar date
Source timezone or timezone-resolution status
Activity type
Distance, duration, elevation, and heart-rate fields when available
Raw-file reference when available
Deduplication status and confidence
Data-quality flags
Calculation/schema version
Use the existing project's storage conventions after inspection. Preserve original imported records rather than silently mutating them. If a timezone cannot be resolved, store an explicit unknown status instead of guessing.

Where:
The existing activity import/model/storage modules identified in docs/IMPLEMENTATION_INVENTORY.md; add migrations or schema files in the project's existing migration directory. Add tests in the existing test directory.

How to verify success:

A clean import produces one canonical record per retained activity.
UTC timestamp, local timestamp, and local date are stored separately.
Source provenance and raw-file references are retained when available.
An unresolved timezone produces a visible data-quality status rather than an assumed timezone.
Existing duplicate handling is represented as metadata, including confidence or review status.
Automated tests cover timestamp conversion, missing timezone handling, provenance retention, and duplicate metadata.
The project's normal test and build commands pass.
Priority: HIGH

3. Add an explicit data-completeness and athlete-confirmation workflow
What to do:
Add data-quality structures and UI/API behavior for:

Suspected duplicate activities
UTC/local-date discrepancies
Missing source files
Unresolved timezone or location
Calendar gaps that require confirmation
Missing activity fields
Import failures
Represent calendar gaps as "data completeness needs confirmation." Do not label them as missed workouts, rest days, or injuries. Provide a way for the athlete to mark a gap as confirmed rest, missing data, or unknown, while preserving the original status and audit history.

Where:
Use the canonical activity layer from Task 2. Add the corresponding service/API and frontend components in the existing project locations. Add documentation to docs/DATA_COMPLETENESS.md.

How to verify success:

A seven-day or nine-day activity gap is displayed as requiring confirmation.
The system does not create a missed-workout record automatically.
The athlete can select a supported confirmation status.
Confirmation records include timestamp, actor, and previous status.
Suspected duplicates and timestamp discrepancies are visible and reviewable.
Tests cover gap detection, confirmation state changes, and protection against automatic missed-workout inference.
Priority: HIGH

Create a repeatable inspection/import command that reports:

Files inspected
Files with GPS coordinates
Files without GPS coordinates
Coordinate validity and coverage
Timestamp fields found
Lap-level records found
Parse failures
Where:
Existing FIT import/parser code and raw data directories. Add the inspection command under the project's existing CLI or scripts convention. Write the report to docs/FIT_DATA_AUDIT.md or the project's generated-report location.

How to verify success:

The inspection command runs against the available source files without modifying them.
The report identifies whether usable GPS coordinates exist.
GPS and lap data are retained when present, with source-file provenance.
Files without GPS are flagged as unavailable rather than assigned a default route.

Automated tests cover at least one file with GPS, one without GPS, and malformed or unsupported input where fixtures are available.

7. Implement versioned, explainable training-load calculations
What to do:
Build a transparent load service that calculates rolling 7-, 14-, and 28-day values for:

Distance
Duration
Elevation
Running intensity
Session RPE load when available
Strength-training stress when available
Keep running and lifting stress separate before optionally presenting a combined view. Store the calculation method and version with every derived result. Mark results conditional when activities or subjective inputs are incomplete. Include an acute-versus-chronic comparison only with clear labeling and limitations; do not present ACWR as a validated injury predictor.

Where:
Add the calculation service to the existing analytics/domain layer. Add versioned calculation documentation to docs/TRAINING_LOAD_METHOD.md and tests in the existing test suite.

How to verify success:

The service calculates all requested rolling windows using local activity dates while retaining source timestamps.
Missing data does not become zero without an explicit documented rule.
Running and strength loads remain distinguishable.
Every result identifies its calculation version and input completeness.
A sudden increase in volume, intensity, elevation, or strength stress produces an explainable flag.
The output explains which records contributed to the result.
Tests cover empty windows, partial data, duplicate exclusion, and a known fixture with expected results.
Priority: HIGH

8. Add provisional training-control recommendations with safety boundaries
What to do:
Implement an explainable recommendation layer for the immediate recovery/reset phase and the following four-week structure:

Week 1: recovery/reset
Weeks 2-3: gradual progression
Week 4: deload
The recommendation logic must support approximately 18-22 miles initially, no maximal intervals, no hill repeats during the immediate reset, a long run below approximately 8 miles during the immediate reset, and at least one full rest day. It must favor approximately 75-80% clearly easy running over the next four weeks and allow pace to slow or walking on climbs when needed.

Use an initial conservative easy HR ceiling around 150-156 bpm only as a configurable provisional value. Label it unvalidated and adjustable for heat, hills, and athlete input. Recommendations must reduce, hold, or progress load based on incomplete data, pain, soreness, sleep, and recovery inputs. Pain or medical symptoms must trigger a clear recommendation for appropriate professional evaluation rather than an injury diagnosis.

Where:
Existing coaching/recommendation domain and UI. Add rules and rationale documentation to docs/TRAINING_CONTROL_RULES.md.

How to verify success:

Recommendations show the rationale and source metrics used.
The immediate reset rules are enforced and visible.
The system does not recommend simultaneous increases in mileage, elevation, running intensity, lifting load, and lifting volume.
Provisional HR guidance is clearly labeled as non-definitive.
Pain or concerning medical symptoms produce escalation language and no diagnostic claim.
Incomplete activity data causes a conditional recommendation rather than false certainty.
Tests cover recovery, progression, deload, high-load, high-pain, and missing-data scenarios.
Priority: HIGH

What to do:
After Task 4 establishes whether usable GPS exists, implement historical weather enrichment using confirmed activity timestamp and location. If GPS is unavailable, implement an athlete location-request workflow or integration boundary; do not use an assumed location.

Store, for each enrichment attempt:

Historical versus forecast type
Temperature
Relative humidity
Dew point
Wind speed
Wind direction
Precipitation
Apparent temperature
Weather-condition metadata
Weather source
Retrieval timestamp
Weather model/version
Location and timestamp matching method
Matching confidence
Failure or unavailable status
Keep forecast retrieval for planned activities separate from historical enrichment and require planned location and time for forecasts.

Where:
Existing integration/service layer. Add weather schemas and migrations in the existing data layer. Add provider configuration through environment variables or the project's established secrets mechanism. Document behavior in docs/WEATHER_ENRICHMENT.md.

How to verify success:

Historical enrichment requires a confirmed activity timestamp and location.
Forecast requests require a planned location and planned time.
Failed or unavailable enrichment is flagged without imputed weather values.
Historical and forecast records cannot be confused in the data model or UI.
Provider, retrieval time, model version, and confidence are stored.
Tests cover missing location, invalid coordinates, provider failure, successful historical enrichment, and successful forecast retrieval using mocked provider responses.
The UI does not claim that Open-Meteo or another weather source was used unless a successful retrieval record exists.
Priority: MEDIUM

Where:
